back: We use the past simple to give an account of a sequence of past events in chronological order [1].
We use the past perfect to refer to an event that happened before the last event in a sequence we have written or spoken about [1].

front: Past simple vs. Past perfect (Context clarity)
back: If the order of past events is clear from the context (e.g., using 'after'), we can often use either tense [1].

front: Continuing a narrative after past perfect
back: Once we understand we are talking about events before another past event, we don't have to continue using the past perfect; we can use past simple [1].
The past perfect is often used in reporting what was originally said or thought in the past simple or present perfect [1].
We use the past perfect (or past simple) to talk about things we intended to do, but didn't or won't do (e.g., 'I had hoped to visit...') [1].
Verbs like 'hope', 'plan', 'intend', and 'want' are commonly used in the past perfect to describe unfulfilled plans [1].
Reported as: 'I was sure that I had met him before' [1].
Reported as: 'She admitted that she had stolen the watch' [1].
Reported as: 'Police said that 225 people had drowned in the recent floods' [1].

front: After Ivan had finished... / After Ivan finished...
back: Both are correct because 'after' makes the sequence of events clear [1].
We use the past perfect to 'step back' to an earlier point from a time already in the past [1].
Reported as: 'I found that the village hadn't changed much' [1].
Both can be used to talk about things intended to do but didn't happen [1].
'I wrote the email, gave the present, and made a mistake'. All in past simple because they follow a timeline [1].
